*"Don't you miss having a strong man's shoulder to lean on?"* Rebecca223 asked, with a hundred-dollar donation. *"Would you give up your business if you met the love of your life?"*

Freya decided to answer.

"A business won't replace a man, and a man won't replace your life's work. Though you don't have to please a business the way you do a lover. And the right business will *always* stand up for you"—here Freya smiled—"which, you have to admit, gives it a distinct advantage over a man."

The chats exploded. The Twitter and Instagram feeds on the side monitors raced by like crazy. The feminist community mobilized in full force, and the feed suddenly bloomed with colorful-haired avatars like an exotic greenhouse. Now it wasn't the assistants, but Freya's fans themselves who were mass-reporting and slinging mud at the right-wingers who had swarmed to the light of her stream from their anonymous loser forums. Right-wingers were always a lot of trouble.

And yet three hundred and eighty... no, three hundred and ninety thousand live viewers were still three hundred and ninety thousand viewers. No matter what they smelled like.

Trolls tried to flood the broadcast with questions like *"Do you give head?"* and *"Try shaving your legs"*: completely unimaginative, but in huge numbers. Stupid sad green frogs started popping up in the chat. Freya kept smiling and selectively answering questions while glancing at her assistants' chat. No matter how you sliced it, the comments set the tone. Still, the moderators' help wasn't needed.

The trolls' moms didn't give them more than five dollars for school lunch. So they were utterly routed by a counterattack from Freya's core audience, which rallied at the call of fan groups on Twitter, TikTok, and Instagram. Moms on maternity leave, nail technicians, and small-town college girls rushed to their idol's rescue. Housewives who, answering the clarion call of the modern economy, had traded their ladles for oversized smartphones. And also men who craved the attention of all the aforementioned women and had therefore started posing as "one of their own," not even noticing how they were blowing twenty bucks a month or more on Freya.

Not the best audience if you're a serious woman sharing the secrets of *real* success, but a loyal one. And in real business, loyalty counts for a lot.

Right before Freya's eyes, the haters' comments were washed away by twenty- and fifty-dollar messages: *"Go, Freya!", "Freya, we love you!", "#Axelsensexuals!"* The stakes were rising fast, and before long, donations under ten dollars weren't even making it onto the screen. At last, the young woman genuinely smiled.
